A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NsDiff research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on nine real-world and two synthetic datasets, component ablations, and prediction showcases in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds pretraining-versus-joint-training results and computational-cost measurements in Appendix B.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds an evaluated alternative that jointly trains the networks without pretraining, whereas v1's specified procedure pretrains the mean and variance estimators. This is a limited training variant; the default architecture, loss, diffusion processes, and inference algorithm remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same nine real-world datasets and linear/quadratic synthetic datasets for the same forecasting tasks. The added training comparison uses ETTh1; neither appendix addition introduces a new population, domain, or input scenario.

E2.justification: TimeGrad, CSDI, TimeDiff, DiffusionTS, and TMDM remain the comparison baselines in the corresponding forecasting experiments. The new efficiency comparison reuses these methods; the pretraining experiment compares NsDiff training variants.

E3.justification: Table 8 introduces an epoch-by-epoch comparison of pretrained and joint training through six epochs. Table 9 adds training/inference time and memory evaluation. The existing forecasting splits, input lengths, prediction horizons, ten-epoch budget, diffusion settings, and sampling procedure remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices B.2–B.3 examine whether pretraining is necessary and how computational costs compare with existing methods. These are targeted supplementary analyses; the original LSNM/noise-schedule ablations, synthetic distribution-shift analysis, and prediction showcases are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seeds {1,2,3} and retain the same uncertainty reporting in Table 5. The added studies introduce no additional seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 3–5 and 7 retain their numerical results. Table 8 adds CRPS trajectories, including epoch-six values of 0.3795 with pretraining and 0.3873 with joint training; Table 9 adds resource measurements. Table 6 reverses the MAE/MSE labels while retaining its numbers: NsDiff's ETTh1 values become MAE 0.523 and MSE 0.594. This changes reported metric assignments, not demonstrated same-setting performance.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the DDPM forward marginal q(Y_t|Y_0): its mean uses sqrt(alpha_bar_t)Y_0 in v3 instead of sqrt(alpha_bar_t)Y_{t-1} in v1. The NsDiff derivations and mathematical arguments in Appendix A remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central claims remain introducing LSNM-based uncertainty modeling and an uncertainty-aware diffusion schedule, with headline improvements of up to 66.3% on real-world data and 88.3% on synthetic data. Local abstract edits and added appendix evidence do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds interpretations of joint training as viable but harder to converge, and discusses computational efficiency and the memory burden of the default mean estimator. Section 4.3 removes the explanation that pointwise distributions are unavailable from a single observation, reducing the stated motivation for the sliding-window variance surrogate.

D1.justification: Table 9 newly discloses measured training/inference time and memory usage. Appendix C's implementation code, MLP configuration, variance-window settings, synthetic-data generators, and code/data access information are retained. Hardware and detailed timing procedures are not supplied for the new measurements.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Chen et al. (2023, 2024), Shi et al. (2023), Jiang et al. (2023), and Xu et al. (2024). Related work modestly expands its discussion of Schrödinger bridges and invariant-measure approaches, while retaining the original positioning around non-stationary uncertainty.

P1.justification: There are localized abstract, pretraining, and inference wording edits. Appendix B changes from Point Forecasting Results to Other Results and Discussions, with subsections for retained point forecasts and the two added studies. The main section order and most exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with clearer framing, multiple inference samples, and an explicit predicted-distribution display. Tables 8–9 are added, Table 6's metric labels change, and Figure 5 moves alongside Appendix D's discussion. Existing empirical plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful evidence about pretraining and computational costs, corrects Table 6's metric labels and the DDPM forward marginal, and clarifies practical tradeoffs. These gains are limited: the efficiency measurements lack hardware/timing details, and removing the pointwise-distribution caveat weakens the explanation of variance estimation. Overall, the added evidence and corrections modestly improve the paper without substantially changing its central validation.
